results.message: What happened to people who gave in during the persecution?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
They were not cast out, and the road back was real. Some sacrificed at the altar; others paid for a certificate saying they had. Both fell, and both were ours. They sat where we sit, and now they wanted to come home. Cyprian told us that when the flock is wounded, the shepherd carries that wound himself. The demand had reached each person alone, and it sorted us into those who stood and those who did not. Both groups still belonged.

What happened to them in practice depended on what they did next. One man, Numidicus, had watched his own wife burn for the faith and was dragged to the fire himself. His daughter searched for his body and found him still alive. Cyprian brought him into the presbyters of Carthage. That is a confessor who stood. For those who gave way, there was a road, and it was walked in the open, under the bishop's own hand. It was not granted on request, and it was not settled in private. The same people who watched the failure received the person back.

glosses.plain_meaning: A certificate is a letter from a confessor, given to a lapsed person. It asks for peace, or says peace is granted. Cyprian wanted each one to name the person. Some named one person and then let in his own people too, without naming them.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, a certificate is a confessor's letter for a lapsed person. It asks for peace, or grants it. Who decides is what we argued over.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener who has just heard about the sacrifice-certificate will assume this is the same document, or a version of it, and will tend to hear 'letter of peace' as a devotional gesture. We mean the opposite document, travelling the opposite way: the sacrifice-certificate proves compliance with the empire and made a person lapsed; this certificate asks peace for that person, or says it is granted. It is administratively real -- issued in thousands, argued over by name, and regulated in writing.
false_friend: the same document as the Decian sacrifice-certificate, rather than the opposite one -- a request to be readmitted, not a record of prior compliance
a devotional or ceremonial gesture rather than an administratively real, regulated instrument issued in the thousands

glosses.plain_meaning: A bishop, for us, is not an officer of some wider institution, dropped into a posting. He is given a people. He preaches to them and baptizes them, and when they fail it is not a problem he manages but a wound he carries. The charge runs both ways: he answers for his flock, and his flock can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, the flock is not the church in general. It is the particular people one bishop is given, in one place. He answers for them, and they can hold him to it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener often hears 'flock' as soft and a little patronizing -- pious language for churchgoers, gentle on the pastor's side, passive on theirs, and 'bishop' as a regional administrator several removes from ordinary life. We do not mean either. The flock is a charge that can be lost, and its failure is reckoned to the one who holds it. Our people are not passive: they elect, they demand, and they can force a bishop's hand. And the bishop is not remote -- he is the man who preached to you himself and knows which of you did not come.
false_friend: a soft, sentimental way of describing churchgoers, with a passive congregation and a gently benevolent pastor
a bishop understood as a remote regional administrator rather than the man who preaches to these people himself and knows who did not come

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, a confessor is one who was interrogated for the Name, did not deny it, and lived. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop's own authority.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, a confessor is someone who was asked to deny the faith, did not, and lived. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener will almost certainly hear 'confessor' as a priest who hears confessions -- the later, Western, sacramental sense -- or a vague honorific for a saintly figure. We mean the opposite direction entirely: not one who hears confession, but one who made confession, under interrogation, at real risk, and survived. The word names what was done to us and what we did not say, and it carries a claim on the church's own decisions rather than an office within its ministry.
false_friend: a priest whose office is to hear other people's confessions, the later, Western, sacramental sense of the word
a vague honorific for any saintly figure, with no specific claim on church authority attached

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised (Doc_01 SS2; lpc.story.election-of-cyprian); banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258 (lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian)

confidence.divergence_note: The regulating voice is Cyprian's throughout, as with every entry in this cluster; the confessors' own certificates survive only in one general letter of theirs to Cyprian (Epistle XVI), which says 'we have granted peace' to all whose conduct has been satisfactory 'in your estimation'; the rest is Cyprian quoting, paraphrasing, and objecting to them (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). 'Thousands' is Cyprian's own word: Hartel's Latin of Epistle XX.2 reads 'libellorum milia', and the translation reads 'thousands of certificates were daily given, contrary to the law of the Gospel'. This record uses his wording.

The dense verbal evidence for this term is Cyprian's own; Augustine's use of the same image is real but far less frequent. Our claim that this is a cross-phase pattern rests on both bishops' own conduct of the office, not on matching word-counts in each phase (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes, Lexicon_Deployment_Index.md SS6).

elements.surface: Cyprian brought him into the presbyters of Carthage.

confidence.divergence_note: The evidence base for this term is essentially one Registry row (the Epistles) read through one lexicon entry, disclosed at generation rather than discovered afterwards (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). A phase bound was established by a check, not assumed: a sweep of all eight vendored Augustine volumes returns twenty occurrences of the stem against roughly 150 in Cyprian's one volume, and none carries this sense -- this term belongs to Cyprian's phase and does not cross into Augustine's.
